data.title: 3 ‘Strong Buy’ Data Center Stocks to Watch After Anthropic’s Record IPO
data.description:
AI developer Anthropic (ANT) began trading on Thursday on Nasdaq. It raised a record $81.34 billion in its initial public offering (IPO), above its earlier target due to strong demand. This has drawn fresh attention to the AI trade. For investors looking for other ways to gain exposure to the industry, analysts remain bullish on three less popular data center-related names: Willdan Group (WLDN), Comfort Systems (FIX), and Graham Corporation (GHM). Each stock carries a Strong Buy rating from analysts with at least 50% upside, according to TipRanks’ Compare Top Data Center Stocks tool.

GHM has rallied the most year-to-date, up 23% to about $77 per share. However, Willdan offers the biggest upside of 78%.

These companies are among the “pick and shovels” of the AI buildout. They provide the physical infrastructure that powers the data center boom.

Willdan Group (WLDN)

Willdan is an American engineering and construction company. It helps companies maximize their energy systems and modernize their electric grids. It also offers consulting on building and safety guidance.

The company’s clients span utilities, government agencies, and private businesses.

Willdan’s shares are currently down about 29% year-to-date. However, analysts continue to rate the stock a Strong Buy and see about 78% upside in the months ahead. This is based on an average price target of $130.

Comfort Systems (FIX)

Comfort provides mechanical, electrical, and plumbing contracting services. The Texas-based firm helps clients install, maintain, and retrofit their heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems.

Comfort Systems’ shares are up about 22% since the start of the year. Interestingly, analysts see room for an even bigger rally. They expect the stock to rally by 67% in the months ahead. This is based on the average price target of $1,849.

Graham Corporation (GHM)

Graham is an American industrial engineering and manufacturing company. The New York-based business makes fluid, power, heat transfer, and vacuum technologies.

Graham produces several items, including condensers, cryogenic pumps, and ejectors. Other products include turbines, generators, cooling systems, and thermal-control electronics. Its products are used in data centers to cool AI systems.

Graham’s shares are up 23% year-to-date to about $77 per share. Analysts see room for another 56% rally over the coming months. This is based on an average price target of $120.50.

data.title: Nvidia Stock Could Plunge to $100, Warns Investor — Here’s Why
data.description:
What started as a promising Thursday for Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors has turned into another disappointing session. After surging nearly 5% earlier in the day, the chip giant has reversed course, falling 3.3% as uncertainty continues to weigh on the broader market. The latest reversal leaves Nvidia shares 38% below their October peak and down 21% since the beginning of 2026. Concerns surrounding its leadership transition, extensive spending commitments, and the sustainability of AI infrastructure investments continue weighing on sentiment.

And if investor Sungarden Investment is correct, the worst may still lie ahead. Despite Nvidia’s already steep losses, the investor believes the stock could tumble all the way to $100 over the next 12 to 18 months. His warning rests primarily on technical indicators and broader market conditions, suggesting that Nvidia’s troubles extend well beyond the controversy surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang.

Sungarden’s bearish outlook begins with a comparison between current trading patterns and previous market downturns. Although Nvidia has recovered from several steep sell-offs over the past decade, the investor believes this episode could prove far more damaging.

“While I always account for the possibility that any stock or ETF can manage yet another big leg up, I think the odds are against NVDA this time,” Sungarden noted.

Sungarden believes institutional selling could continue overwhelming buying interest, preventing a lasting recovery despite Nvidia’s technological advantages. The investor also points to deteriorating liquidity, suggesting that large investment funds may be reducing their exposure to leading tech companies.

Another concern involves the financial relationships supporting the industry’s rapid expansion, where investments move between cloud providers, developers, and semiconductor manufacturers. Sungarden points out that these arrangements could become problematic for Nvidia if financing slows, while Huang’s departure introduces additional uncertainty surrounding strategic direction.

However, the investor considers broader trading mechanics more important than any individual controversy, especially when examining heavily weighted equities like Nvidia during prolonged market downturns.

“In a liquidity-driven unwind, the generals are always the last to get taken out. And their drop is the steepest,” Sungarden explained.

Essentially, Sungarden argues that Nvidia’s dominant position within passive portfolios could become a liability when investors withdraw capital from index funds. Those withdrawals could increase selling pressure on heavily weighted stocks like Nvidia, potentially creating additional downward momentum regardless of underlying financial performance.

His Nvidia chart analysis also reveals deteriorating momentum, with several important moving averages already broken and successive rallies failing to establish stronger price levels.

Ultimately, Sungarden offers a particularly bearish forecast for investors expecting Nvidia to recover its previous valuation: “To $100, more likely than back to $240, its previous peak level, over the next 12-18 months.” (To watch Sungarden Investment’s track record, click here)

With Nvidia trading near $147 on Thursday, that scenario implies another 32% downside, potentially extending an already costly retreat for long-term holders.

While Sungarden sees further losses ahead for Nvidia, most Wall Street analysts remain bullish on the company’s long-term prospects. Nvidia currently has a Moderate Buy consensus rating, based on 30 Buys, 13 Holds, and just one Sell assigned over the past three months. The average 12-month price target stands at $232.59, representing 59% upside from current levels. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: ‘A Blessing in Disguise,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Nvidia’s leadership crisis has kept investors on edge for the past couple of weeks. It began when reports surfaced that Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman U.S. officials suspect of spying for China. He resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and chip stocks were hit hard on Monday when worries about his exit came on top of new U.S. export rules. A better-than-expected quarter on Tuesday didn’t stop Nvidia’s slide either.

Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has been one of the AI stocks affected by the fallout. And despite the shares gaining today as Anthropic goes public, the stock still sits roughly 38% below its June peak.

While the market evidently did not like Huang’s resignation and the board’s refusal to consider his return, investor Chetan Woodun thinks the Huang affair could turn out to help the American AI trade, and Micron with it.

The argument starts in Washington. If investigators find that Beijing was trying to get at sensitive chip technology, the affair becomes a national security case. That could bring Republicans and Democrats together behind domestic chipmaking and AI infrastructure, and behind tighter limits on what reaches China. A first step has already happened. On Nov. 16, the Commerce Department said exporters now need a license to send advanced AI chips to overseas data centers that rent computing power to Chinese firms. Huang had long argued for selling to China, so the investor thinks his exit could make tougher rules easier to pass.

That matters for Micron because its high-bandwidth memory (HBM) goes inside the same AI accelerators Washington wants to keep away from China. Woodun also likes that Micron doesn’t depend on a single buyer. Its HBM3E chips are used in AMD’s Instinct MI350 line, and the investor thinks AMD could gain ground if Nvidia struggles under new leadership. Micron’s latest annual report shows that no customer made up 10% of sales in fiscal 2026. A year earlier, one customer accounted for 17%.

Demand looks solid. Speaking at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin on Wednesday, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said 75% of Micron’s 2027 output is already sold and that talks have moved on to 2028. He expects memory supply in 2027 and 2028 to be even tighter than this year. Even so, the stock trades below 5x forward earnings, and Woodun thinks Micron has earned a higher multiple.

The investor does see risks. Memory has a long record of booms followed by painful busts. The Fed raised rates in September and is expected to raise them again in December, which hurts debt-funded customers like CoreWeave. Data centers are also drawing criticism for the strain they put on power grids and water supplies. China worries Woodun less. Memory isn’t the main target of U.S. export rules, and Micron expects China to make up a single-digit share of revenue in fiscal 2027.

In the end, Woodun’s view is that one company’s leadership crisis doesn’t derail the AI spending cycle, and that it may even strengthen it by keeping China further behind.

Accordingly, Woodun rates MU stock a Buy. (To watch Woodun’s track record, click here)

So do most Street analysts. Based on 28 Buys vs. 1 Hold, consensus views this stock as a Strong Buy. Going by the $1,624 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for a 118% premium. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Someone’s Betting Against AMD Stock, and This Investor Sees a Better AI Bet Elsewhere
data.description:
When Nvidia lost its founder and CEO last week, the money leaving its shares stayed in the AI chip trade. Much of it went to Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO), the two names usually pitched as the alternatives. A week on, one of them has a problem of its own.

AMD fell as much as 11% on Thursday after short seller Hunterbrook disclosed a bet against the stock. Hunterbrook alleges that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept receiving updated AMD firmware, and it questions how much AMD finances the customers buying its chips. AMD pushed back, telling Bloomberg that Hunterbrook’s claims “misrepresent” its business practices and relationships and that it follows US export control rules.

The latest news makes a useful backdrop for a recent analysis by an investor using the moniker of Millennial Dividends (MD), who, before the short report was released, wondered which of the two is better placed to benefit from Nvidia’s troubles. MD is less focused on the leadership change than on Nvidia’s roadmap. Kyber, the rack meant for 2027’s Rubin Ultra chips, has reportedly slipped to 2028 because of a hard-to-make circuit board. Rubin Ultra itself has reportedly been cut from four compute dies to two. MD thinks the CEO exit could drag those delays out.

AMD is doing fine on its own, with third-quarter revenue up 45% year over year to $13.4 billion and guidance for more than 80% growth in 2027. If hyperscalers need capacity in 2027 that Nvidia can’t deliver, MD sees them buying more MI450 chips as “capacity insurance,” even though moving code off Nvidia’s CUDA software is costly. Still, AMD is unlikely to become the main supplier, and more competition could squeeze chip prices. Whether that actually lifts AMD’s revenue growth is, in MD’s view, anyone’s guess.

Broadcom’s setup is cleaner. Fiscal third-quarter AI chip revenue more than tripled YoY to $16.7 billion, and CEO Hock Tan is targeting about $115 billion in AI revenue for fiscal 2027. Broadcom co-designs the custom chips, or XPUs, that hyperscalers buy instead of Nvidia GPUs, under deals with Google through 2031 and Meta through 2029. Its Tomahawk Ethernet switches go into Nvidia clusters and custom ones alike, so a delayed Nvidia rack makes little difference to it. The risks are a gross margin guided down to about 73% from 78% a year earlier, as XPUs take a bigger share of sales, and a concentrated customer base.

Valuation widens the gap. Broadcom trades at about 18x its fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $19.47. Even after Thursday’s drop, AMD sits near 27x its 2027 estimate of $17.69. MD sees little room for error in AMD’s price. AMD could still come out ahead if it takes real share from Nvidia, but Broadcom gets paid whichever way Nvidia’s roadmap goes. That’s why MD is holding off on buying any more AMD shares right now and keeps Broadcom as the top pick. (To watch Millennial Dividends’ track record, click here)

On the Street, both these stocks are considered Strong Buys. Over the next year, AMD is expected to gain 34%, given the average target clocks in at $652.18. AVGO’s average target lands at $514.86, implying the shares will climb by 45% over the 12-month timeframe. (See AMD stock forecast or AVGO stock forecast)

data.title: VOO vs. DRAM: AI Chip Bet or Broad Market — Which ETF Wins?
data.description:
Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) and Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) offer very different ways to invest in the stock market. While VOO tracks the S&P 500, DRAM gives investors direct exposure to memory chip stocks. Using TipRanks’ ETF Comparison Tool, we compared VOO and DRAM to find the best ETF for investors.

VOO vs. DRAM: Which ETF Holdings Offer the Most Upside?

According to TipRanks’ unique ETF Analyst Consensus, which is based on a weighted average of analyst ratings for each ETF’s holdings, VOO has a Moderate Buy rating.

VOO has an average price target of $844.70, implying 24.83% upside. Among its holdings, SanDisk (SNDK)  has the highest upside potential at 160%, followed by Micron (MU) at 118%.

DRAM’s top holdings by upside potential include Kioxia Holdings Corporation (JP:285A) at 372% and SanDisk at 160%.

DRAM or VOO – Key Differences

VOO is much cheaper to own than DRAM. It charges an annual fee of just 0.03%, or $3 for every $10,000 invested. DRAM charges 0.65%, which works out to $65 a year on the same investment. DRAM’s higher fee reflects its focus on memory chip stocks. VOO is the cheaper option for long-term investors who want broad market exposure.

DRAM is much more concentrated than VOO. Its top 10 holdings make up 71.26% of the portfolio, compared with just 37% for VOO. This means DRAM is heavily exposed to a handful of companies. VOO spreads its money across hundreds of U.S. stocks.

DRAM also carries higher risk with a beta of 3.87, while VOO’s beta is 1.00.

VOO and DRAM – Major Holdings

VOO holds 507 stocks with total assets worth $1.04 trillion. VOO’s top 5 holdings are Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), and Alphabet (GOOGL).

DRAM ETF includes firms that make DRAM, HBM, NAND flash, and SSD technologies. DRAM owns 19 stocks, with major holdings such as SK Hynix (SKHY), Samsung (SSNLF), SanDisk, and Seagate (STX).

Conclusion

VOO is the safer, long-term option because it is broadly diversified and grows steadily across the whole U.S. market. On the other hand, DRAM is a higher-risk, higher-reward ETF focused on AI memory and semiconductors, so it can rise faster in strong chip cycles but also fall harder when the sector slows down.

data.title: Nvidia or Rocket Lab: Jim Cramer Says One Stock Is Too Cheap, Avoid the Other
data.description:
Wall Street has a new AI darling, while Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is still struggling to regain its appeal. As investors celebrate Anthropic’s highly anticipated Nasdaq debut, the chip giant remains 36% below its October high.

Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has experienced an even steeper fall, losing 64% of its value since reaching its May peak. While the space tech company continues expanding its operations and securing new contracts, concerns about spending requirements and delays involving its next-generation Neutron rocket have weighed on investor sentiment.

For investors wondering whether these sell-offs represent buying opportunities, Jim Cramer has made his views clear. The Mad Money host believes Nvidia can be left out of portfolios for now, while Rocket Lab deserves another look after its steep retreat.

Nvidia Has Lost Its Appeal

For years, investors knew exactly who was steering Nvidia through the AI boom. That certainty disappeared with Jensen Huang’s departure, leaving the company navigating one of its most challenging periods without the executive who became synonymous with its success.

Yet, while Nvidia’s leadership has changed, the financial commitments made during Huang’s tenure remain immense. The company’s latest earnings revealed that supply commitments had climbed from $279 billion to $390 billion, reflecting extensive agreements supporting future infrastructure requirements. These commitments increase Nvidia’s exposure to future demand fluctuations, adding financial risks for the executives guiding the company through its next chapter.

Meanwhile, Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut has given investors another opportunity to participate in the AI boom. With the Claude developer attracting considerable enthusiasm, Cramer believes some investors would rather pursue that opportunity than wait for Nvidia’s leadership situation to improve.

“You don’t need to own Nvidia,” Cramer said, arguing that investors want Jensen Huang back rather than waiting for interim CEO Colette Kress and the board to complete their search for a permanent replacement.

He added that investors have effectively voted Nvidia off their portfolios, suggesting that Anthropic currently offers a more appealing destination for capital.

Despite Cramer’s reservations, Wall Street remains broadly bullish on Nvidia’s longer-term prospects. Nvidia carries a Moderate Buy consensus rating based on 30 Buys, 13 Holds, and one Sell assigned over the past three months. The average 12-month price target of $232.59 implies about 52% upside from current levels. (See NVDA stock forecast)

Rocket Lab Has Become Too Cheap

Rocket Lab faces its own challenges, although Cramer believes the recent sell-off has created an opportunity for investors willing to accept additional risk.

The company’s latest quarterly results demonstrated continued expansion, supported by growing demand for launch services and space systems. Rocket Lab reported a backlog of approximately $3.6 billion, providing visibility into future revenue as commercial and government customers expand their space-related investments.

However, the postponement of its Neutron rocket’s debut until 2027 has raised concerns about execution and future spending. The larger launch vehicle represents an important part of Rocket Lab’s strategy to compete for more valuable missions, making its development timeline particularly important for investors.

Cramer nevertheless sees value following the stock’s steep retreat: “This Rocket Lab has gotten too cheap,” he said, adding, “I think you have a good one. It’s a spec.”

Rocket Lab’s lower share price appears to have done little to weaken analysts’ expectations for its future performance. Wall Street assigns RKLB a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 15 Buys and 3 Holds over the past three months. The average 12-month price target stands at $95.41, representing 78% potential upside. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Market Already Knows,’ Says Investor About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has spent the past year showing that strong quarters and a rising share price don’t always go together. Its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday followed the same pattern. Results beat expectations and the outlook came in stronger, yet the shares gave up an early jump on Wednesday and closed lower. This time there was an extra weight on the stock. It was the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and the question of who runs Nvidia next is still unresolved.

The board says Huang won’t be back, and Bloomberg reports it is now courting Arm CEO Rene Haas. The stock now sits more than a third below its October record.

That gap between the business and the stock is where investor Vladimir Dimitrov puts his focus. He has no quarrel with the latest results, but he thinks the share price already reflects near-term expectations, so the useful signals sit in what the guidance implies.

Growth is a good example. Revenue more than doubled year over year for a second straight quarter, and management raised its early fiscal 2028 forecast to about 75% growth, from 70%. Dimitrov doesn’t think that changes much. He believes the market is bracing for several years of slowing growth, which is why Nvidia’s price-to-sales multiple has kept shrinking through a run of beats. The shares now trade at less than 11 times forward earnings. He sees the second quarter as the likely peak. YoY growth slipped from 106% then to 103% in the third quarter, and the guide implies about 90% for the fourth.

Margins follow a similar path. Gross margin topped guidance last quarter, but Nvidia expects it to bottom at 71%–72% this quarter before settling at 72%–73% in fiscal 2028, while operating expenses climb to nearly $11 billion. Further out, memory costs could ease and lift margins back toward 75%, but Dimitrov sees pricing power and hyperscaler demand as risks.

That last one worries him most. By his numbers, combined capex at Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle jumped 118% YoY in the third quarter and now exceeds operating cash flow for four of the five. He sees a real chance that 2026 marks the top for spending by some of Nvidia’s biggest customers. He also flagged interim CEO Colette Kress saying on the call that the company is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees,” which he reads as a sign the easy gains are behind it.

Dimitrov’s base case is that growth, margins and hyperscaler demand all peak in 2026. In his view, the stock can keep posting great numbers and still do no better than the broader market.

As such, he rates NVDA a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Dimitrov’s track record, click here)

Thirteen Street analysts are also on the sidelines here, while an additional 30 Buys and 1 Sell add up to a Moderate Buy consensus view. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 53%, given the average target clocks in at $232.59. (See Nvidia stock forecast)

data.title: Fortinet (FTNT) vs. Zscaler (ZS): Which Cybersecurity Stock Offers More Upside?
data.description:
Fortinet (FTNT) and Zscaler (ZS) stand to gain as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warns of rising cyber threats to U.S. critical infrastructure, though Wall Street sees higher upside in one. The warning indicated that criminals are using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) to carry out more cyberattacks and identify potential targets. The comments come as U.S. officials also highlighted threats to transportation, healthcare, water, and energy systems.

These cybersecurity stocks take different approaches, with Fortinet providing network security and firewall solutions, while Zscaler focuses on securing cloud access, applications, and data. We compared the two stocks using the TipRanks Stock Comparison tool to see which offers more upside, according to analysts. The tool can also help to compare stocks based on market cap, P/E ratio, Smart Score, dividend yield, and more.

Is FTNT Stock a Buy?

Fortinet is a U.S.-based cybersecurity company that provides network security and firewall solutions for businesses and government organizations. Its Security Fabric platform is designed to protect networks, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments. It has recently pushed into AI security, launching the FortiGuard Inline AI Security Service, which adds AI-specific inspection and guardrails for FortiGate customers through a cloud-delivered service. Founder, Chairman, and CEO Ken Xie said Q3 reflected strong execution and broad-based demand across the entire portfolio, which let the company raise its 2026 billings guidance for the third time this year.

In Q3 2026, revenue grew 20% year-over-year to $2.08 billion, product revenue rose 37% to $765 million, and billings grew 29% to $2.34 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) climbed 23% to $0.91. For full-year 2026, Fortinet now expects revenue of $8.125 billion to $8.215 billion and billings of $9.568 billion to $9.718 billion, with EPS of $3.54 to $3.58. The board also authorized an additional $1.2 billion in share repurchases.

On TipRanks, Fortinet has a ‘Perfect 10’ Smart Score. The average stock price target of $150.76 implies a 10.07% upside. 18 analysts rate the stock a Hold, seven rate it a Buy, and four analysts rate it a Sell. Overall, FTNT has a Hold consensus rating.

Is Zscaler a Buy, Sell, or Hold?

Zscaler provides cloud-based zero-trust security through its Zero Trust Exchange platform. The platform helps organizations control access to applications and data based on user identity, device security, and business policies, rather than relying on traditional network-based defenses. CEO Jay Chaudhry said the agentic AI era is quickly becoming the most significant opportunity in the company’s history and that Zscaler is working toward a $10 billion ARR target.

In Q4 2026, revenue was $898.2 million, up 25% year-over-year, and adjusted EPS was $1.19 against estimates of $1.09. Full-year FY26 revenue rose 25% to $3.353 billion. Zscaler also expects $30 million to $33 million in restructuring charges, mostly in the first half of FY27. Also, growth in customers with ARR above $1 million has slowed over recent quarters.

Zscaler has a TipRanks Smart Score of 7. It has a Strong Buy consensus, with 30 of the 36 analysts covering the stock rating the stock a Buy. The average ZS stock price target of $239.50 suggests a 12.22% upside from recent price levels.

Conclusion

The growing use of AI is changing both the nature of cyberattacks and the tools companies need to defend against them. Fortinet is building on its network-security and firewall expertise, while Zscaler is positioning its cloud-based Zero Trust platform for a world where users, devices, and applications operate beyond traditional network boundaries. The data above offers a side-by-side view of where each company stands today. Wall Street currently sees more upside in ZS.

data.title: ‘Follow the Cash,’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
On the day Wall Street finally gets its hands on a frontier AI lab, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) shareholders have reason to look past the party. Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq today after pricing above its marketed range in the largest IPO ever. OpenAI, the lab that matters most to Oracle, is still private and is reportedly aiming for a 2027 listing.

That matters because Oracle’s growth plans depend heavily on OpenAI being able to keep raising money. OpenAI accounts for nearly half of Oracle’s backlog, and the ChatGPT maker’s latest private round has reportedly reached $15 billion, half of its original goal. Anthropic just showed that public investors will hand an AI lab $81.3 billion in one go, but OpenAI can’t tap that pool yet.

Oracle shares currently trade almost two-thirds below their September 2025 record.

Keith Noonan, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, sees that reliance on a single customer as a big reason Wall Street has lost its nerve on the stock.

Oracle closed its fiscal first quarter on Aug. 31 with $664 billion in remaining performance obligations, meaning work customers have signed up for that hasn’t turned into revenue yet. At least $300 billion of that is widely thought to come from OpenAI. The investor points out that the contract terms aren’t public. Oracle would probably collect cancellation fees if OpenAI pulled back, but a fee is only worth something if the customer can pay it. In his view, Oracle has staked its future on OpenAI growing into its commitments. Noonan adds that this kind of exposure bites harder in AI infrastructure, where data centers cost a fortune to build and run.

So far, the results show no strain. First-quarter revenue rose 30% year over year to $19.3 billion, cloud sales jumped 62% to $11.6 billion, and adjusted EPS climbed 30% to $1.92. At today’s price, the stock trades at roughly 14 times the $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS management is guiding to for fiscal 2027. Noonan agrees those numbers make Oracle look cheap, but he doesn’t think they tell the full story.

The cash flow statement is less comfortable. Oracle brought in $23 billion in operating cash during the quarter but spent about $28.5 billion on capex, leaving free cash flow at negative $5 billion. Because a data center counts as an investment on the balance sheet rather than a cost on the income statement, the investor notes, reported earnings understate how much money is going out the door. Oracle is plugging the gap with borrowing and share sales. It carries about $125 billion in debt, plans $90 billion to $95 billion in capex this fiscal year, and will probably keep spending big after that.

For Noonan, fast growth and a low multiple don’t outweigh a debt-funded build-out tied this closely to one customer, and he sees Oracle stock as riskier than its earnings make it look. (To watch Noonan’s track record, click here)

Most on the Street, however, take an optimistic stance here. Based on a mix of 28 Buys, 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. At $241.83, the average price target implies shares will gain 111% in the months ahead. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Don’t Be a Fool,’ Says Investor About Anthropic Stock
data.description:
What a difference one blockbuster IPO can make to Wall Street’s mood after several turbulent weeks. With Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) arriving on Thursday, investors seem willing to overlook recent tech losses, the controversy surrounding Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang, fears about excessive AI expenditures, and uncertainty stemming from the Democrats’ midterm victories.

The excitement surrounding the Claude developer is understandable, considering its $83 offering price, record $81.3 billion IPO, and valuation of about $1.5 trillion. With the broader market surging, investors appear ready to embrace what could become one of the most closely watched listings in history.

Yet, investor Rafa Oliver believes the enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic may be getting ahead of financial reality. Despite recognizing the company’s technological achievements and rapid expansion, Oliver sees serious risks for anyone purchasing shares at current valuations.

Oliver makes his central concern clear in his analysis, writing, “My doubt is the price, and it comes from how I see the business: Anthropic sells work that gets cheaper with every new model, it has two rivals with deep pockets, and to keep up with them, it has to rent its computers years before it knows how much it will sell.”

Anthropic has already committed about $900.9 billion toward computing infrastructure, creating considerable financial obligations should customer demand fall short of expectations.

Meanwhile, competition from OpenAI and Google could limit pricing flexibility, making sustained profitability harder to achieve. Oliver estimates that annual revenue could reach $766.6 billion by 2036, giving the Claude creator a commanding 68% share of his projected industry opportunity.

However, even those assumptions fail to support the original $74 IPO midpoint, let alone the final $83 offering price. According to his calculations, operating margins would need to improve far beyond historical levels to justify even the earlier valuation.

Computing costs represent another concern, having consumed 48.1% of sales during Anthropic’s strongest reported quarter. Oliver estimates that this figure would need to fall to 26.2% for the earlier pricing assumptions to make financial sense.

Employee compensation introduces further complications, with stock-based awards potentially reducing intrinsic value by $31.29 per share. Such dilution could erode returns for long-term holders, regardless of how successfully Anthropic expands its operations.

Oliver also believes investors should consider how much future growth is already reflected in today’s valuation. His model assigns the company a fair value of just $46.26 per share, which would represent about 44% downside from the final $83 IPO price.

And when it comes to deciding whether investors should participate in the highly anticipated debut, Oliver leaves little room for interpretation: “On listing day, I would not buy.” His conclusion reflects his belief that Anthropic’s valuation already exceeds what its financial prospects can justify. data.title: Nvidia vs. Intel: One AI Stock Is Worth the Drama, the Other Isn’t Worth the Wait, Says Investor
data.description:
For a while, the only thing Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) had in common was that they both made chips.

Nvidia rode the AI boom to become one of the world’s most valuable companies, while Intel spent years trying to repair its business. Now they share a problem: shareholders who aren’t sure what comes next. Nvidia released its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, its first since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, and the stock still fell the next day. Intel’s slide deepened after it issued a weak outlook in late October.

Nvidia’s revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion, and interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%. On the same call, though, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. That came only hours after Huang said he would be honored to return.

Nvidia stock now hovers near its lowest level since around June 2025. This week Intel was hit by a shareholder lawsuit and by a filing showing that Nvidia sold about a quarter of its Intel stake. Intel shares sit about 60% below their June peak.

So, where to now for these two embattled chip giants?

An investor going by the moniker of The Curious Analyst (TCA) has two very different reads on these stocks.

On Nvidia, TCA thinks the leadership drama is already reflected in the share price. The stock fell sharply when Huang stepped down, but the board’s refusal to bring him back drew a much milder reaction. The investor takes that as a sign the market trusts Kress. In TCA’s view, investors can now see what Nvidia looks like without its founder, and the danger of relying on one person has faded.

The business case rests on the product cycle. Vera Rubin added nearly $20 billion in revenue from the previous quarter, and the investor expects growth to hold up as it ramps alongside Blackwell Ultra. TCA also expects Nvidia to use up its remaining buyback authorization of about $227 billion by the end of fiscal 2028, as management has said it will, which would shrink the share count. Assuming a net margin of about 50%, TCA’s fiscal 2028 EPS estimate lands at $16.12.

Nvidia trades at roughly 10 times forward earnings, far below its historical range. TCA thinks a multiple in the low 20s, near the sector median, would be reasonable. The investor also sees an upside that the model leaves out for now. SpaceX caught Starship’s upper stage for the first time last weekend, and TCA thinks cheaper launches could eventually create demand for AI hardware and data centers in space.

The main risks are a slowdown in AI spending and the chance that investors won’t pay a higher multiple without Huang. Still, TCA notes that Nvidia impressed the market in the middle of an AI selloff and a leadership crisis, and sees that as evidence the company is on solid ground.

Bottom line, TCA reiterated a Strong Buy rating on NVDA stock. (To watch The Curious Analyst’s track record, click here)

The investor is far less comfortable with Intel. Its fourth-quarter revenue guidance midpoint of $15.5 billion fell well short of the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and the stock lost more than a quarter of its value the next day. For TCA, the bigger problem is profitability. Intel’s trailing 12-month net margin is about -20%, and right now the market has little patience for cash burn.

TCA’s model assumes revenue grows about 9% next year and allows for a recovery to a 6% net margin, roughly the sector median. That gives a 2027 EPS estimate of $0.78, less than half the Wall Street consensus of $1.79. The one thing TCA finds encouraging is Intel’s long-term earnings growth outlook. Even so, Intel trades at about three times Nvidia’s forward multiple.

The risks are more dilution after a stock sale of more than $20 billion in August, margins that could slip again, and a multiple investors may stop paying.

While TCA is no fan of the stock right now, the investor stops short of rating it a Sell. TCA argues that the post-earnings collapse already made shareholders pay for one disappointing quarter, and Intel still has a real role in PCs, data centers and AI. It has come back from tough stretches before. The investor wants to see fourth-quarter results and the 2027 outlook before deciding which way to go.

For now, TCA rates INTC stock a Hold (i.e., Neutral).

On the Street, NVDA claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating, while its $232.59 average price target points to 12-month returns of 54%. INTC is rated a Hold, although, interestingly, its $90.93 average target suggests shares will gain 66% over the one-year timeframe. (See NVDA stock forecast or INTC stock forecast)

data.title: Nike (NKE) Targets a Turnaround with Ambitious Fiscal 2031 Goals
data.description:
Nike (NKE) is targeting a major turnaround with ambitious Fiscal 2031 goals, and the stock’s current valuation reflects only a fraction of the long-term earnings potential those goals imply. Shares of the sportswear maker have fallen more than 40% in 2026, impacted by a mix of company-specific issues such as negative revenue growth and weak earnings momentum, as well as macro headwinds like high energy prices that weigh on discretionary consumer spending.

In response, the company has laid out a plan to generate $5 billion in incremental revenue and an adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $3–$3.50 by Fiscal 2031 (the company’s financial year ends in May).

On near-term numbers, the stock doesn’t look cheap. The elevated 26.8x multiple on management’s expected Fiscal 2027 EPS of about $1.35 suggests the market is already pricing in some earnings recovery. However, the picture changes against the longer-term target, implying that the market is giving credit for only part of the expansion projected for the years after Fiscal 2027.

I rate Nike a speculative Buy. While hitting ambitious financial targets is far from certain, the shares appear somewhat undervalued should Nike achieve the $3.25 midpoint of its Fiscal 2031 EPS outlook. Coupled with the company’s aspiration to return $12 billion to shareholders as the turnaround unfolds, I think the shares offer enough value at current prices.

Nike’s New Fiscal 2031 Targets

Nike used its Investor Day, held on November 17, 2026, to announce its new “Full Stride Ahead” strategy. Its key elements include ambitious Fiscal 2031 targets, most notably $5 billion in incremental revenue and an adjusted EPS of $3–$3.50.

Let us use the $42.8 billion analyst estimate for Fiscal 2027 as a starting point to evaluate management’s top-line ambitions. Assuming Nike hits its $5 billion incremental revenue target, we see that annual revenue growth should amount to just under 3% per year, indicating limited volume growth and sales rising largely in line with inflation. While this may seem rather unambitious, it would represent the company’s fastest top-line expansion since Fiscal 2023, when sales increased 9.65%.

For earnings, the projected improvement is much more pronounced. Using Nike’s forecast of adjusted EPS of about $1.35 in Fiscal 2027, the $3–$3.50 adjusted Fiscal 2031 EPS target implies about 25% annual earnings growth at the $3.25 EPS midpoint. I think this is quite ambitious given the modest revenue aspirations outlined above.

Before we dive into the details behind these numbers in the next section, I believe the key takeaway for readers is that the “Full Stride Ahead” strategy is centered around earnings growth, with revenue expansion playing a secondary role in my opinion. That said, I think the sales targets in particular are quite achievable, supporting my Buy rating on the shares.

Nike’s Revenue and Earnings Drivers

Now that we have seen the key numbers behind Nike’s new strategy, let’s discuss how the company plans to get there. Given the modest projected revenue expansion of marginally below 3% per year over the “Full Stride Ahead” horizon, I think achieving margin improvements will ultimately determine Nike’s turnaround success.

For Fiscal 2027, the company anticipates delivering an adjusted operating margin of about 6%. By the end of Fiscal 2031, the number should be closer to 12%–14%, implying a dramatic improvement. Avenues for margin improvement include simplifying and standardizing processes to improve execution and productivity, implementing integrated planning across demand, inventory, supply, and financial decisions, and building a more flexible, responsive supply network.

Nike also targets greater use of technology and artificial intelligence (AI) to improve decision-making, speed, and efficiency. As such, the road to higher margins for Nike entails both improving the efficiency of existing processes and making the most of new technologies such as AI to drive incremental improvements.

While margin expansion is expected to do the heavy lifting for EPS growth, Nike also expects a turnaround in sales momentum. Here, the company is focusing on 23 priority countries, which will drive over 90% of the anticipated $5 billion revenue growth. Nike anticipates higher sales by scaling breakthrough innovations into platforms that reach more athletes across more sports, as well as working with marketplace partners to tailor product assortments and experiences to local athletes.

To sum up, Nike’s earnings growth is likely to come primarily from efficiency gains and associated margin expansion, with higher revenues playing a complementary role. While the absolute level of margin improvement may seem too ambitious at first, achieving 12%–14% operating margins is certainly doable for an efficiently run company, supporting my Buy rating on Nike.

Nike’s Valuation

Nike shares trade at 26.8x expected Fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS of $1.35, implying the market is giving the company some credit for anticipated medium-term earnings growth. For comparison, the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 index (RSP) trades at a much lower valuation of about 16.6x forward earnings.

I think the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 is a good benchmark for Nike, as the company’s market cap has slumped to only $53 billion after declines in the 2026 share price. This is well below the large-cap stocks that dominate the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 index (SPX), which trades at a higher valuation.

My view on Nike is that it will outperform equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 peers only if it hits at least the midpoint of its $3-$3.50 adjusted EPS target for 2031. This potential outperformance comes as Nike may deliver about 25% annual EPS growth over the next four years, notably above the approximate 8.5% EPS growth I expect for the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500.

At the $3.25 midpoint of the Fiscal 2031 EPS outlook, the current share price works out to roughly 11x earnings, suggesting the bigger earnings gains planned for later years are only partly reflected in today’s valuation. This supports a speculative Buy rating on Nike, as the market appears to be giving the company very little credit for its medium-term earnings recovery.

Another positive factor in the Nike investment case is management’s commitment to its dividend, forecasting $12 billion in cumulative dividend returns between Fiscal 2027 and Fiscal 2031. Investors should note, however, that the $0.41 per share quarterly dividend is not covered by projected Fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS of $1.35. The silver lining is that dividend coverage should steadily improve as Nike executes its turnaround plan.

Wall Street’s Take on Nike

On Wall Street, Nike has a Hold consensus rating, based on nine Buy, 18 Hold, and 10 Sell ratings over the past three months. The 12-month average Nike price target is currently $36.73, implying 1.17% upside.

Conclusion

After disastrous 2026 share price performance, Nike is implementing the “Full Stride Ahead” strategy to improve sales and profitability. While the strategy does envisage some revenue expansion, the bulk of the anticipated earnings growth is projected to come from higher margins.

The market remains somewhat skeptical of Nike’s turnaround, with the shares trading at 26.8x expected Fiscal 2027 earnings. While this may seem high relative to immediate peers in the equal-weight Invesco S&P 500 index, it gives the company little credit for its projected nearly 25% EPS growth over the next four years.

I rate Nike a speculative Buy, as the shares should outperform peers if the company hits its new financial targets. That said, the new strategy carries execution risks, so outsized returns are far from guaranteed.

While Fiscal 2031 is still far off, Nike aims to return $12 billion to shareholders in the meantime, potentially making it an interesting play for income investors as the company works on its turnaround. As such, I think Nike stock may appeal to income investors as well as growth investors.

data.title: LLY Stock: Is It Still a Buy at Record Highs?
data.description:
Eli Lilly (LLY) has delivered impressive growth in 2026, but with shares near record highs, LLY is no longer a Buy, in my view. The drugmaker’s shares have gained nearly 31% year-to-date, far outpacing the S&P 500 (SPX), and have held firm even as investors rotate out of richly valued technology names. LLY jumped about 6.6% on the day it reported blowout Q3 results, with revenue up 39% to $24.4 billion on surging demand for its leading weight-loss drugs, Mounjaro and Zepbound. Management also raised its full-year revenue guidance by $5.5 billion at the midpoint.

Analysts are raising their forecasts, reflecting confidence in Lilly’s growth prospects. However, the company faces a potential glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) price war in 2027, which could put pressure on pricing even as demand grows. While I remain impressed by Lilly’s execution, I believe much of the good news is already priced in, and I rate the stock a Hold.

Lilly’s Weight-Loss Franchise Dominates the Obesity Market

While Eli Lilly’s near-term upside looks capped at current valuations, there is no doubt that its weight-loss franchise dominates the obesity market. Mounjaro and Zepbound were once again the stars of Lilly’s Q3, accounting for more than $16 billion in combined revenue. Mounjaro sales climbed 65% to $10.72 billion, while Zepbound sales rose 49% to $5.35 billion.

International demand is a growing driver: Mounjaro became the first medicine in China to surpass $1 billion in revenue in its first full year, helped by its inclusion on China’s National Reimbursement Drug List. In the U.S., access continues to widen through the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, which has generated more than 500,000 prescriptions since launching in July, with seven out of ten new Bridge patients starting on a Lilly obesity medicine. Even so, much of this operational momentum appears reflected in the stock’s current valuation, reinforcing a Hold stance as pricing headwinds build into 2027.

Foundayo and a Deep Pipeline Extend the Runway

My Hold rating accounts for the fact that Foundayo and a deep clinical pipeline extend Lilly’s growth runway well into the next decade, even if near-term upside looks limited. Beyond its injectables, Lilly is building its next leg of growth. Foundayo, its once-daily obesity pill, targets patients who prefer a pill over weekly injections. Management said approximately four in ten U.S. patients starting an oral obesity medicine now choose Foundayo.

The drug is also rolling out internationally, with recent launches in the U.K., Mexico, and Saudi Arabia. Longer term, Lilly’s pipeline includes Retatrutide, which has delivered up to 22.6% weight loss in Phase 3 trials and is slated for a U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) filing in Q1 2027, and Eloralintide, both potential successors to Mounjaro and Zepbound.

Still, with those late-stage candidates still quarters away from commercialization and the stock trading near all-time highs, waiting for a better entry point makes sense.

The Price War and the Pill Race

The price war and the pill race reinforce my decision to stay on the sidelines. Despite its strong growth, Lilly is increasingly relying on selling far more doses at lower prices. In Q3, worldwide volumes rose 53% while net realized prices fell 15%. The trade-off was starkest outside the U.S., where volume surged 76%, but prices dropped 29%, largely due to Mounjaro’s inclusion on China’s reimbursement list. That pressure could intensify in 2027, as Novo Nordisk (NVO) plans to cut U.S. list prices for Wegovy and Ozempic to $675 per month starting January 1.

Pricing is not the only 2027 headwind; the quality of Lilly’s 2026 results also deserves scrutiny. Q3 revenue of $24.4 billion included roughly $900 million in one-time benefits, about 4% of the total, mainly from Jardiance milestone payments and favorable rebate adjustments, and Lilly has said no further Jardiance milestones remain. Because 2027 growth will be measured against a base lifted by these non-recurring items, Lilly’s upcoming guidance will show how much of its momentum is underlying.

Lilly is also playing catch-up in oral obesity drugs. While Foundayo’s share of new oral starts is rising, its revenue still trails Novo’s Wegovy pill by a wide margin: $184 million in Q3 versus roughly $811 million for Novo. The key question is whether Foundayo’s prescription momentum can translate into meaningful revenue and lasting patient adherence. Pills are expected to widen the obesity market into primary care, so falling behind here puts long-term share at risk.

LLY’s Valuation

LLY’s valuation already reflects much of the good news. LLY trades at about 45x trailing earnings, nearly double the S&P 500’s 24.4x and above the sector median P/E of 26.44x. Even Wall Street sees limited room from here: the average price target implies just about 10% upside, suggesting much of Lilly’s growth is already reflected in the share price. Upcoming catalysts, including the Retatrutide filing and growing contributions from Lilly’s oncology, immunology, and neuroscience acquisitions, could help justify the premium in 2027.

Is LLY a Good Stock to Buy?

LLY has a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 22 Buys, one Hold, and one Sell assigned in the past three months. The average LLY stock price target of $1,520 implies about 10% upside potential. Price targets range from a low of $940 to a Street-high $1,700 from Jefferies. Jefferies recently lifted its price target to a Street-high $1,700 from $1,610.

LLY Remains a Leader in Weight Loss Stocks

Eli Lilly enters 2027 as the clear leader in obesity care, with surging volumes, a promising successor in Retatrutide, and fast-growing businesses outside GLP-1s. The risks are real, though: falling realized prices, a pending Novo price cut, and a lag in oral drugs.

In my view, Lilly’s scale should let it win a price-for-volume battle, but at today’s valuation, I rate LLY a Hold and would look to buy on pullbacks rather than chase the stock at record highs. Investors should watch Lilly’s 2027 guidance for how it plans to handle pricing, along with the Retatrutide filing in early next year.

data.title: Anthropic Stock Is Finally Here. What It Means for AI, According to Dan Ives
data.description:
Until now, if you wanted to own a piece of the companies building frontier AI models, you had to buy something else first: a search giant, a cloud provider or a chipmaker. That changes this morning. Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT), the company behind the Claude chatbot, is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq. It is the first major U.S. AI lab to have a ticker of its own.

The timing could have been better. Tech stocks have had a bruising few weeks, and Jensen Huang’s sudden exit from Nvidia last week shook confidence in the whole AI trade. Even so, demand was strong enough for Anthropic to upsize the deal and price it at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range it had marketed. At that price, Anthropic is raising $81.3 billion, which puts it on track to be the biggest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX’s listing in June.

One of the best-known tech bulls on Wall Street is Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives, who thinks the debut tells investors a lot. “In our view this is a clean read on demand,” the 5-star analyst wrote. In his view, investors were hungry to own a frontier AI developer of this size, and the pricing shows it. He expects OpenAI to follow in 2027.

What stands out most to the analyst is that, for the first time, investors can value a U.S. frontier lab on its own, with no advertising or space business attached. He also points to who is buying in. Nvidia and Google each took $10 billion of a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price, with AMD and other chip and cloud suppliers also on the list. To Ives, the spending the hyperscalers laid out earlier this month and the computing power Anthropic is signing up for are “the same dollars viewed from both ends.”

Anthropic’s filing shows roughly $900 billion in compute commitments stretching over many years. Ives sees that as a long-term demand signal for chipmakers and the clouds that host them. Investors can now read it in a public document instead of piecing it together from capex guidance.

Ives, who ranks among the top 3% of Street stock experts, doesn’t pretend the picture is simple. Third-quarter revenue grew more than twelvefold year over year, but prices are falling and compute bills are landing before the matching revenue is booked. Anthropic made an operating profit in Q2 and slipped to an operating loss in Q3. Ives believes the stock’s direction will depend on which of those quarters turns out to be the real run-rate.

Still, the analyst calls the IPO “a big near-term win for the tech sector,” one that should reassure nervous investors that the AI growth story still has legs. The market is in “a very turbulent, white-knuckle period,” Ives wrote, but that doesn’t change his view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion will go into AI infrastructure over the next few years, with Anthropic a “central player in the buildout.” (To watch Ives’ track record, click here)

This talked-about stock already has 3 positive analyst reviews, making the consensus rating a Strong Buy. (See ANT stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia vs. Micron – Why Top Analyst Sees More than 110% Upside in One AI Chip Stock
data.description:
Micron (MU) and Nvidia (NVDA) are both benefiting from rising AI demand. RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri has reiterated Outperform ratings on both stocks. His $230 price target for Nvidia implies 52.36% upside. For Micron, his $1,500 target points to 112.68% upside, making Micron his more bullish pick.

After meeting with Micron’s management, Pajjuri remained positive on the stock. He wrote, “We walked away comfortable with our positive stance and view the recent pullback as an excellent opportunity.”  For Nvidia, he pointed to strong chip demand and its product roadmap.

Pajjuri is a five-star analyst on TipRanks, ranked #272 out of 12,578 analysts. He has a 59% success rate and an average return of 30.20% per rating. Here is why he sees more upside in Micron.

Micron’s Tight Memory Supply Could Drive More Upside

Pajjuri expects memory supply to stay tight in 2027 and 2028. After meeting with Micron’s investor relations and treasury teams, he said AI demand and rising HBM use could keep supply below demand. He also sees fewer gains from chip upgrades adding to supply limits.

Micron has already secured much of its future supply. RBC estimates that about three-quarters of its 2027 supply is allocated. It also noted that long-term supply deals cover more than 35% of Micron’s revenue through 2030. Pajjuri noted that these deals give the company better demand visibility. He added, “we see no signs of demand weakening currently.”

Micron has also signed more Supply Commitment Agreements (SCAs). It added 10 new deals in the fourth quarter, taking the total to 26. The agreements cover about 35% of its 2027 DRAM and NAND shipments. They are legally binding and include set pricing bands.

At about 4.2 times estimated 2027 earnings, Pajjuri sees room for Micron’s valuation to rise.

Nvidia’s Strong AI Chip Demand Supports RBC’s Bullish View

Pajjuri also remains bullish on Nvidia after its latest results. The company’s results and outlook came in above market expectations. RBC has raised its FY28 revenue growth outlook to about 75%, from 70% earlier.

Nvidia’s supply commitments have also risen. Pajjuri sees this as a sign of strong demand and confidence in future sales. He believes demand is still well ahead of supply. In his note, he said “demand is significantly outpacing supply.” He also sees Nvidia’s product roadmap as a strength over the next three years.

Nvidia has $227 billion left under its share buyback plan. However, Pajjuri flagged a risk around the company’s leadership. The board has ruled out bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO. He said this “could raise concerns about talent retention.” Even so, RBC sees an attractive risk-reward for Nvidia.

Micron vs. Nvidia: Which Stock Has More Upside?

According to TipRanks data, Micron has a Strong Buy consensus rating, while Nvidia has a Moderate Buy rating. Micron has an average 12-month price target of $1,624.42, implying 130.33% upside. Nvidia has an average price target of $232.59, suggesting 54.08% upside. (See MU Stock Forecast and NVDA Stock Forecast.)

data.title: SpaceX vs. Nvidia: Only One AI Stock Is a ‘Strong Buy’ with 85%+ Upside Ahead of Anthropic’s IPO
data.description:
Anthropic’s IPO puts two major AI stocks in focus: SpaceX (SPCX) and Nvidia (NVDA). The Claude maker priced its shares at $83, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion ahead of its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, November 19. Both firms have direct ties to Anthropic. Nvidia is investing in the AI company and supplies the chips used to run its models. SpaceX, in turn, provides the computing power Anthropic needs.

The IPO comes at a tough time for both stocks. SpaceX is down 11.96% so far this year, while Nvidia has pulled back sharply from its early October peak following Jensen Huang’s departure, leaving shares down about 16.6% year-to-date. Even so, Wall Street sees room for both stocks to rise. SpaceX has a Strong Buy rating and nearly 89% upside. Nvidia has a Moderate Buy rating and about 50% upside.

SpaceX’s $120.5 Billion Anthropic Deal Could Grow Further

SpaceX has agreed to provide Anthropic with computing power worth up to $120.5 billion through 2029. Anthropic disclosed the deal in its IPO filing. Once all the planned capacity is in place, the AI firm expects to pay about $3.1 billion per month. SpaceX expects to deliver the full capacity by December 2026.

Anthropic is already a major customer for SpaceX. Bloomberg reported that it accounted for 34.5% of SpaceX’s revenue in the third quarter of 2026. It was also the company’s largest single customer.

The deal could also expand. Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, SPCX CEO Elon Musk said Anthropic was likely to keep renting computing power from SpaceX. He added that the AI firm’s most likely plan was to seek another 10 gigawatts of capacity. Anthropic has not confirmed this figure.

However, the current deal carries some risk. The contracts have initial periods during which they cannot be canceled. Once these periods end in January and March 2027, either side can end the agreements with 90 days’ notice. This means SpaceX may not receive the full $120.5 billion.

Nvidia’s $10B Anthropic Investment and Compute Deal

Nvidia has both an investment and a chip supply link with Anthropic. It has agreed to invest $10 billion in the AI firm through the private placement tied to the IPO. This gives Nvidia a stake in the fast-growing company.

 Nvidia also supplies the GPUs used in Anthropic’s computing deal with SpaceX. As Anthropic expands its AI services, it may need more GPUs from Nvidia. This could support chip sales.

Still, Nvidia sells GPUs to many other AI firms and data center operators. It also faces competition from other chip makers and custom AI chips from cloud providers. This gives Nvidia a wider customer base beyond Anthropic.

SPCX vs. NVDA: Which AI Giant Offers More Upside Now?

Nvidia carries a Moderate Buy consensus. NVDA average 12-month price target of $232.59 implies nearly 50% upside from current levels. By contrast, SpaceX enjoys stronger backing on Wall Street, earning a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 28 Buys, five Holds, and one Sell. SPCX average price target points to about 89% upside over the next year.

data.title: Nebius Stock’s (NBIS) Q3 Sell-Off Looks Like an Opportunity
data.description:
Nebius (NBIS) stock’s Q3 sell-off looks like an attractive opportunity, with shares down almost 64% from their 52-week high. The artificial intelligence (AI) cloud infrastructure provider disappointed investors with another capacity delay, but the underlying business momentum tells a very different story. Rather than pulling back, customers are locking in much larger, multi-year commitments. As CEO Arkady Volozh emphasized on the earnings call, “The demand for AI is real and substantial.”

Q3 2026 revenue surged 571%, and new contract economics improved. I understand the concerns about financing this enormous expansion. Yet customers’ willingness to help fund it makes me more confident. Thus, I rate NBIS stock a Buy.

A Strong Quarter Got Overshadowed

Nebius’ strong Q3 results got overshadowed by another capacity delay. Investors were already questioning Neocloud financing and the sustainability of AI spending. Nebius then shifted some expected revenue into early 2027 because third-party capacity was delayed. Management now expects 2026 revenue near the low end of its $3.0–$3.4 billion range.

Its $7 billion-plus annualized revenue milestone moves from December to February. That is disappointing, although the customer contracts behind the delayed capacity remain intact.

More importantly, the company showed considerable progress. Revenue reached $980.8 million, up 68% sequentially, while AI Cloud revenue grew 643% year-over-year. Group adjusted EBITDA reached $465.8 million, and AI Cloud’s adjusted EBITDA margin was 53.2%. Annualized revenue run rate rose 113% sequentially to $6.4 billion.

Q3 included $325 million of nonrecurring partner revenue. Excluding that contribution, revenue still exceeded four times last year’s total. Customers have also signed over $12 billion of contract value since Q3 began.

The improving contract terms are what impressed me most. Prepayments on Q3 contracts lasting at least a year covered more than 100% of associated capex. That compares with 50%–60% in Q2. Management’s revenue-based payback estimate for comparable contracts improved to 19 months from 22 months. Customers are signing longer agreements at higher prices, helping Nebius recover its spending faster.

I believe this is really important for a company buying expensive graphics processing units (GPUs). Customer funding reduces its dependence on the next debt deal or equity raise.

The Growth Outlook Still Looks Excellent

Meanwhile, the growth outlook still looks excellent heading into 2027. Management expects $12–$13 billion of revenue, roughly four times this year’s level. Four new sites began generating revenue in Q3, with more capacity arriving during Q4. Nebius plans to add over 1 GW annually, increasingly through owned sites. That should give it more control over delivery and operating costs.

Management expects prepayments and investment-grade contract financing to cover 75%–85% of 2027’s $40–$45 billion capex. Microsoft (MSFT) and Meta (META) agreements support that financing strategy. Nebius has over $40 billion of similar committed revenue and ended Q3 with $7.4 billion in cash.

Nvidia’s (NVDA) results on November 17 further strengthened my confidence in that outlook. The chipmaker’s Data Center revenue grew 110%, and Rubin achieved Nvidia’s fastest product ramp. Nebius was among the providers already running Rubin racks. Nvidia also described extraordinary neocloud demand, with $32 billion of commitments extending into 2032 and beyond. Its support depends on financing being secured and capacity becoming operational.

I see those conditions as sensible discipline. They require projects to work before Nvidia’s commitments take effect. So they don’t suggest customers have stopped wanting compute.

Rental pricing offers further evidence. Nebius raised selected on-demand GPU rates roughly 17%–21% from October 1. Across Nvidia’s customer base, some Hopper contracts renewed at up to twice the prior price. B300 rental rates have risen over 60% since introduction. Higher prices on heavily used equipment improve the potential return on each installed dollar.

Nebius is also building services on top of GPU rentals. Token Factory approaches a multi-hundred-million-dollar revenue run rate, with contract value increasing 17-fold sequentially. Managed inference gives existing customers another reason to spend on its platform. Over time, that could make the business more valuable than a basic compute rental operation.

NBIS’ Earnings Could Catch Up Quickly

The market is struggling to value Nebius stock, but I believe earnings could catch up quickly if the company delivers the planned expansion. The stock is now trading at 36x consensus 2028 earnings per share (EPS) of $2.95. That falls to 15.7x 2029 EPS of $6.80. Losses expected through 2027 make today’s P/E less useful. The question is whether new capacity can produce the profits those later estimates imply.

Management targets pre-tax breakeven in Q4 2027. I think that rising rental prices and stronger prepayments make that goal more credible to me. Its full-stack cloud platform also provides ways to earn more from existing customers. If revenue reaches $12-$13 billion next year, earnings could scale rapidly as infrastructure fills. I consider Nebius one of the better-positioned neoclouds for that transition.

Of course, the risks remain substantial. Further construction delays could increase financing needs and dilution. Large customers account for considerable revenue, while GPU replacement costs will consume cash.

Customer advances bring future service obligations, and EBITDA excludes depreciation and financing costs. An eventual supply glut could also reverse today’s pricing gains. This is a speculative investment, but Q3 gave me stronger reasons to accept those risks.

Is NBIS Stock a Buy?

Wall Street rates NBIS a Moderate Buy, based on nine Buys, two Holds, and one Sell. The $260.90 average price target implies about 144% upside. Several analysts lowered their targets after Q3, reflecting the delivery setback.

Conclusion

Nebius still needs to bring capacity online on schedule. Meanwhile, customers are committing more money upfront and accepting higher prices. That is encouraging evidence for both demand and future profitability. I think the sell-off gives investors an attractive opportunity, provided they can tolerate the risks of this enormous buildout.
data.author: Nikolaos Sismanis
